Cottage Pie, Done Properly

Cottage pie is one of the most practical dishes in British home cooking. Beef mince in a savoury gravy, covered with mashed potato, baked until the top is golden. This website is devoted to that one dish: the classic recipe, the variations worth knowing, and the small details that decide whether yours turns out rich and firm or watery and bland.

If you have come to cook, start with the recipe. If you want to understand the dish first, read on.

What is cottage pie?

Cottage pie is a baked dish of minced beef cooked in gravy, topped with mashed potato. The filling is made on the hob. The pie is then assembled in an oven dish and baked, so the potato crisps and browns on top while the filling bubbles gently underneath.

Two parts, one dish. The filling should be savoury and only just loose enough to spoon. The topping should be soft inside with a ridged, golden surface. When both parts are right, a portion holds its shape on the plate instead of spreading.

Cottage pie is also a forgiving dish. The filling can be made in advance. The whole pie reheats well. Leftovers freeze. That reliability is a large part of why it has stayed in British kitchens for so long.

One point of accuracy, because it causes endless confusion: the name follows the meat. Cottage pie is made with beef. Shepherd's pie is made with lamb. Modern cooks sometimes swap the terms, and some use “cottage pie” for any mince under mash. On this website the traditional distinction is kept, because it helps you find the recipe you actually want.

Cottage pie versus shepherd's pie

The two dishes are built the same way. They differ mainly in the meat, and in the seasonings that suit each meat.

Point of comparisonCottage pieShepherd's pie
Traditional main meatBeef minceLamb mince
Filling base (shared components)Onion, carrot and celery in a beef gravyOnion and root vegetables in a lamb gravy
Typical seasoningThyme, bay, Worcestershire sauce, tomato puréeRosemary or thyme; sometimes a little mint
Typical toppingMashed potato, sometimes with cheeseMashed potato; swede or other root mash also appears
MethodShared: mince filling simmered, topped with mash, baked

Everything else — the dish, the assembly, the baking — is shared. If you can make one, you can make the other by changing the mince and the stock to match.

A word of caution about history. Cottage pie is often described as a way of using up leftover roast meat, and that is plausible. Exact dates and a single neat origin story are harder to prove than recipe books sometimes suggest. This site sticks to what can be stated with confidence: it is a long-established British dish of minced meat in gravy under mashed potato, named for the meat it contains.

Expect the names to be used loosely elsewhere. Supermarkets, pubs and ready-meal ranges do not all keep the distinction, and a “cottage pie” on a menu may occasionally turn out to contain lamb. That is precisely why the distinction is worth keeping at home: when you cook it yourself, the name on the recipe tells you which meat, which stock and which herbs you need before you start shopping.

The ingredients, and what each one does

The full quantities are on the recipe page. This overview explains the roles, so you can judge substitutions sensibly instead of guessing.

The filling

Beef mince is the centre of the dish. Standard mince gives a rich result. Leaner mince gives a lighter one, but needs its flavour built carefully, because there is less fat to carry it. Whichever you buy, brown it properly. Colour on the meat is flavour in the finished pie.

Onion, carrot and celery form the base. Onion brings sweetness. Carrot brings sweetness and body. Celery brings a savoury background note that you would miss if it were gone. All three are chopped small, so they soften into the gravy rather than sitting in lumps. Garlic is used briefly and gently; it should support the beef, not dominate it.

Plain flour thickens the gravy. It is stirred into the pan before the liquid goes in, which coats it in fat and stops it forming lumps. Tomato purée adds depth and a little acidity; a spoonful is enough, and it should not make the filling taste of tomato.

Worcestershire sauce adds savoury sharpness. It contains anchovy, which matters for fish allergies and for some dietary adaptations — the variations page covers what to use instead. Beef stock becomes the gravy; hot stock keeps the pan at temperature and helps the flour thicken evenly.

Thyme and a bay leaf are the classic herbs here. They suit beef and stand up to a long simmer. Frozen peas go in near the end: they add colour and sweetness, and they only need to heat through.

The topping

Floury potatoes — Maris Piper or King Edward are the usual British choices — mash light and fluffy. Waxy potatoes mash dense and can turn gluey. The variety matters more than any gadget.

Butter gives richness and flavour. Warm milk loosens the mash to a consistency that spreads without slumping; cold milk cools the potatoes and makes the mash heavier work. Salt and pepper are not optional details: under-seasoned mash is the commonest reason a cottage pie tastes flat, because the topping is half the dish.

Cheese on top is optional. Grated mature Cheddar gives a savoury, well-browned crust. The pie is complete without it.

The method in brief

The recipe page gives the full method with quantities, timings and cues to follow while you cook. This is the shape of it, in five stages.

  1. Brown the beef. Cook the mince in a hot pan until it is well coloured and its liquid has cooked away. This stage decides much of the flavour.
  2. Build the base. Soften the onion, carrot and celery. Add garlic, flour, tomato purée and Worcestershire sauce.
  3. Simmer the filling. Add hot stock and herbs. Simmer until the gravy coats the back of a spoon and a spoon drawn across the pan leaves a brief trail. Stir in the peas. Taste and season.
  4. Make the mash. Boil the potatoes until a knife slides in without resistance. Drain, steam dry, then mash with butter and warm milk. Season generously.
  5. Assemble, bake and rest. Spoon the filling into an oven dish. Cover with mash, seal it to the edges, ridge the surface with a fork, and bake until golden with the filling bubbling at the edges. Rest the pie before serving, so portions hold together.

Each stage has a failure mode, and they are all fixable. Watery filling, lumpy mash, a pale top — the recipe page works through each one, and the variations page covers changing the dish on purpose rather than by accident.

Practical tips that make the biggest difference

Of everything on this website, these five points change results the most. The recipe page's tips section covers the common mistakes in full.

Reduce the filling properly. Most disappointing cottage pies fail here. If the filling looks like soup in the pan, it will be soup under the mash. Simmer it until it is thick enough to mound slightly on a spoon.

Dry the potatoes before mashing. Drain them, return them to the hot pan for a minute, and let the steam escape. Wet potatoes make loose mash, and loose mash sinks.

Season both halves. Taste the filling. Then taste the mash. Fix each one on its own — seasoning only the filling leaves the top half bland.

Seal and ridge the top. Spread the mash to the edges so the filling cannot bubble up the sides. Ridge it with a fork: the ridges brown, and browned ridges are where the texture is.

Rest the pie. A short rest out of the oven lets the filling settle, so portions come out cleanly instead of sliding. The pie stays hot — resting is not the same as letting it go cold.

Making ahead, storing and reheating

Cottage pie suits being made in advance, which is one reason it appears in so many weekly meal plans.

In advance: the filling keeps well and its flavour improves overnight in the fridge. The assembled pie can also wait in the fridge before baking. The recipe page gives the detail, including what happens to the baking time when the pie starts cold.

Leftovers: cool leftovers promptly — ideally within one to two hours — and refrigerate them at 0–5°C. Eat them within two days. Reheat only once, until the pie is steaming hot all the way through, including the centre. These timings follow Food Standards Scotland and Food Standards Agency guidance; the recipe page links to the official sources.

Freezing: the filling freezes on its own, and the assembled pie freezes whole. Defrost in the fridge and cook within 24 hours of defrosting. Freeze in portions if you usually reheat for one or two people — a portion defrosts and reheats far more evenly than a whole dish.

A safety point worth repeating: reheating is not a way to rescue food that has been stored too long. If leftovers have sat in the fridge beyond two days, throw them away rather than reheating them harder.

The dish, the oven and your equipment

You do not need special equipment for cottage pie. You need the right-sized dish, and it matters more than most recipe books admit.

The dish. The filling and topping need room to sit in a layer that heats evenly. Too small a dish gives a deep pie that bubbles over and heats unevenly. Too large a dish gives a thin pie that dries out. The recipe page states the dish size its quantities were written for — use it, or scale the quantities to the dish you have.

The hob work. The filling is made in one large, wide pan. Width matters: a wide pan lets the liquid reduce, while a narrow, deep saucepan traps steam and slows everything down. If your pan is small, brown the mince in batches — crowded mince steams in its own liquid instead of browning, and the flavour difference is obvious in the finished pie.

The oven. Cottage pie is baked in a moderately hot oven so the top browns in roughly the time the filling takes to bubble through. Every recipe on this site gives both conventional and fan temperatures, because the two differ and guessing wrong by twenty degrees changes the result. The pie is ready by sight as much as by the clock: deep golden ridges, filling bubbling at the edges, and a top that feels set rather than soft. The middle shelf gives the most even result; a dish placed too high browns before the centre is hot.

What to serve with cottage pie

Cottage pie contains meat, potato and vegetables in one dish, so it needs little alongside it. What it benefits from is contrast: something green, something sharp, or something with a different texture.

Green vegetables are the classic choice. Peas are already in the pie for most people, so look beyond them: buttered cabbage, spring greens, green beans or broccoli all work. Cook them simply — the pie is rich, and the vegetables are there to cut through it.

Pickles and sharp sides suit the dish better than most people expect. Pickled red cabbage, a spoonful of piccalilli or a simple dressed salad gives acidity that a gravy-rich plate lacks. Extra gravy divides households; if you serve it, serve it on the side and keep it thinner than the filling's own gravy. And bread for the plate juices is unglamorous and entirely reasonable.

What the dish does not need is more potato in another form. Chips or roast potatoes beside cottage pie are a duplication, not an accompaniment. If you want a bigger meal, add vegetables and a pudding, not a second helping of the topping on the side.

Common questions

Yes. Make the filling, or assemble the whole pie, and keep it in the fridge until you are ready to bake. The section above covers storage times, and the recipe page covers baking from cold.

No. Cheese is a popular addition, not part of the definition. The pie is complete with plain mash, well seasoned and properly browned.

The main recipe

Cottage Pie Recipe

Cottage pie is a baked dish of beef mince in gravy, topped with mashed potato. The filling is savoury and rich, with onion, carrot and celery softened into the sauce. The topping is plain mashed potato, forked into ridges and baked until golden.

It is a straightforward dish to cook at home. Most of the work is simple preparation: chopping vegetables, browning mince and boiling potatoes. The oven does the last stage while you clear up. Cottage pie traditionally uses beef; shepherd's pie traditionally uses lamb. The method is much the same for both, but the meat is different, and so is the name.

This recipe serves four people generously. The filling is thick enough to spoon out in tidy portions, and the mash sits on top as a separate layer rather than sinking into the gravy.

Kitchen tested: cooked exactly as written by the site owner in October 2026 — it turned out as described. Times are a guide; ovens vary, so use the cues in each step. The formulation was also cross-checked against published reference recipes (NHS Healthier Families and the British Heart Foundation). Author: Michael · Published / updated: [Date — to be confirmed at launch]

The Recipe

Serves4
Preparation20 min*
Cooking1 hr 10 min*
Total1 hr 30 min*

* Times are a guide — ovens vary, so judge each stage by the cues in the steps as well as the clock. Most of the cooking overlaps: the filling simmers while the potatoes boil. Oven: 200°C conventional / 180°C fan / Gas Mark 6.

Scaling changes ingredient quantities only. It does not change oven temperatures, cooking times or the dish size — those may need separate adjustment. See Scaling the Recipe below.

Equipment

  • A large frying pan or wide, heavy casserole — room for 500g of mince.
  • A large saucepan for the potatoes; a colander; a potato masher; a wooden spoon and a fork.
  • An ovenproof dish of about 2.5 to 3 litres, roughly 20 × 30 cm.
  • A baking tray to stand the dish on, to catch any drips if the filling bubbles over.

The dish size matters. Too small, and the layers are deep and slow to heat through. Too large, and the filling spreads thin and can dry out. Aim for the filling to sit about 2.5 cm deep before the mash goes on, giving a finished pie about 4.5 to 5 cm deep.

Ingredients — for the beef filling

Ingredients — for the mashed potato topping

Optional ingredients

Method

Two parts of this method overlap, and that is deliberate. The potatoes (Steps 6 to 8) are cooked while the filling simmers (Step 4), not after it. When the filling goes on to simmer, move straight to the potatoes — that overlap is how the total time works.

  1. Brown the mince. Heat the oil over a medium-high heat. Add the mince, break it up, and spread it out rather than piling it in the middle. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes until browned all over with no pink remaining. If the pan looks crowded, brown in two batches — packed mince releases liquid and boils in its own juices instead of browning. Spoon off any large amount of fat, leaving a little behind.
    Cue: the mince should smell savoury and roasted, not steamed.
  2. Soften the vegetables. Turn the heat to medium. Add the onion, carrots and celery and cook for 7 to 8 minutes, stirring now and then. Add the garlic for the final minute.
    Cue: the onion should look soft and translucent; the carrot and celery should lose their hard, raw edge. Garlic should smell fragrant, not bitter.
  3. Add flour and tomato purée. Sprinkle the flour over everything, stir in and cook for 1 minute to cook out the raw taste. Add the tomato purée and Worcestershire sauce, stir through, and cook for another minute.
    Cue: the purée darkens slightly and coats the mince.
  4. Add stock and simmer. Pour in the hot stock, add the thyme and bay leaf, and season lightly. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally. Do not boil hard.
    Cue: the gravy should coat the mince like a sauce, not surround it like soup. A spoon drawn across the pan should leave a trail that fills in slowly. If it is still thin, simmer 5 more minutes without a lid.
  5. Finish the filling. Stir in the frozen peas and cook for 2 minutes. Take the pan off the heat, fish out the bay leaf, and taste. Add salt, pepper or Worcestershire sauce if needed — this is your last easy chance to fix the seasoning. Leave the filling to stand while you finish the mash.
    Cue: the filling should stop steaming fiercely. A boiling-hot filling melts the base of the mash and blurs the layers.
  6. Cook the potatoes. While the filling simmers, peel the potatoes and cut them into similar chunks, about 4 cm across. Cover with cold water, add a good pinch of salt, bring to the boil, then simmer for 15 to 20 minutes.
    Cue: a knife should slide into the largest chunk with no resistance, and the chunk should feel as if it might break apart.
  7. Drain and dry. Drain thoroughly in a colander, tip the potatoes back into the hot, empty pan, and put it over a low heat for about 1 minute, shaking gently once or twice.
    Cue: steam rises off the potatoes and the surfaces look matte and floury, not shiny and wet. Wet potatoes make wet mash.
  8. Mash. Take the pan off the heat, add the butter and mash until there are no lumps. Pour in the warm milk a little at a time, beating as you go. Stop when the mash is smooth and soft. Season and taste.

    If you are using them, stir the pinch of nutmeg or the teaspoon of English mustard into the mash now, along with the butter and before the milk goes in. Both are optional. The pie is complete without either.

    Cue: the mash should hold its shape on a spoon without being stiff. You can always add more milk; you cannot take it out.
  9. Assemble. Heat the oven to 200°C conventional / 180°C fan / Gas Mark 6. Spoon the filling into the dish and spread it level. Spoon the mash on top in large dollops, starting around the edges and working inwards, then spread it gently to the sides so it seals the filling in. Run a fork across the whole surface to make ridges, peaks and grooves. Scatter the optional cheese over the top now, if using.
    Cue: those rough forked edges are what turn crisp and golden.
  10. Bake. Stand the dish on a baking tray on the middle shelf. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes.
    Cue: the top is golden brown in places and the gravy is bubbling up around the edges. If the filling bubbles but the top is still pale, give it 2 to 3 minutes under a hot grill, watching closely.
  11. Rest and serve. Leave the pie to stand for 5 to 10 minutes. The filling settles and thickens slightly, so portions spoon out neatly instead of running across the plate. Serve straight from the dish, standing it on a mat or board.

Recipe notes. Season in stages — stock varies a great deal in saltiness, and you cannot remove salt once it is in. Check the centre is properly hot before serving: steady bubbling right around the edges, not just in one corner. A pie baked from chilled needs longer — see Making Ahead below.

Ingredients and what each one does

Beef mince

The mince is the base of the dish and provides the savoury depth the gravy builds on. Fat content makes a real difference. Very lean mince, such as 5% fat, gives a lighter filling but can taste dry after a long simmer. Mince at around 10 to 15% fat stays moister and browns well. Neither choice is wrong: with leaner mince, be careful not to over-reduce the gravy; with fattier mince, spoon off the excess fat after browning. Whichever you buy, brown it properly — grey, steamed mince gives a flat-tasting filling whatever else you add.

Onion, carrot and celery

These three form the flavour base. Onion brings sweetness once it softens, carrot adds a little sweetness and colour, and celery gives a savoury background note that is hard to name but easy to miss. Cut them small and evenly: large chunks of carrot stay hard in the time available and make the filling awkward to spoon. Garlic supports the same base and should be noticeable but never dominant.

Tomato purée, stock and thickening

Tomato purée adds depth, colour and gentle acidity; two tablespoons is plenty, and cooking it briefly in the hot pan removes the sharp, metallic taste of raw purée. Stock is the liquid of the gravy and a large part of its seasoning — stock cubes and pots are usually saltier than fresh stock, so season in stages and taste again at Step 5. The plain flour, stirred into the fat before the stock goes in, thickens the gravy with a soft, rounded texture and is the traditional thickening for this kind of filling. Cornflour is the alternative for a gluten-free version and behaves differently; see Substitutions.

Worcestershire sauce and herbs

Worcestershire sauce adds a savoury, slightly sharp background flavour; one tablespoon is enough, as more can push the filling towards a pickled taste. Note that it traditionally contains fish, usually anchovy — that matters for anyone avoiding fish, and for a vegetarian version. Thyme suits beef and stands up to simmering; dried thyme is reliable, fresh is milder. The bay leaf works quietly in the background and must come out before assembly.

Potatoes, butter and milk

Floury potatoes make the best mash for a topping. Maris Piper and King Edward break down as they cook, mash smoothly and take up butter and milk well. Waxy and salad potatoes hold their shape instead, which is useful in a salad but leaves mash lumpy or gluey. If you are unsure what you have bought, check the bag — most supermarket potatoes are labelled with variety and best use. Butter gives the mash flavour and a softer texture; warm milk loosens it evenly, whereas cold milk cools the potatoes and can make the mash heavy. Cream can replace some of the milk for a richer topping, but it is not necessary.

Cheese

Cheese is optional, not essential, and traditional versions often have none. Mature Cheddar is the usual choice: 50g has enough flavour to be noticed and browns well. Scatter it over the forked surface, where it will crisp, rather than mixing it through the mash.

How to make the beef filling well

Preparing the vegetables

Dice the carrot and celery to roughly the size of a pea, and chop the onion finely, as it will soften and partly melt into the sauce. Small, even pieces cook at the same rate and distribute through the filling, so every spoonful has some vegetable in it. Prepare everything before the pan goes on — browning mince needs your attention, and it is easy to burn garlic while you are still chopping celery.

Browning the mince effectively

Browning is a chemical change, not just a colour change. Hot, dry contact with the pan creates the deep savoury flavours a simmer alone never produces. Three things make it happen: the pan must be properly hot before the mince goes in; the mince must be spread out, not heaped; and you must leave it alone for a minute or two at a time rather than stirring constantly, so the surfaces in contact with the pan can actually brown. Break up large clumps early. Beyond that, patience does more than stirring.

Avoiding overcrowding and managing fat

Overcrowding is the most common reason mince steams instead of browning. 500g fits a large frying pan, but only just; if your pan is medium-sized, split the mince into two batches and return everything to the pan afterwards. If liquid pools around the mince, pour it off into a jug, keep browning, and add it back with the stock. After browning, if there is a visible pool of fat, spoon most of it off and leave roughly a tablespoon behind — the vegetables cook in it and the flour needs some fat to coat it. With lean mince there may be almost none to remove, so add a small extra drizzle of oil before the vegetables go in.

Simmering to the right consistency

How thick should cottage pie filling be? It should coat the mince like a sauce, not surround it like a soup. Simmer gently and uncovered for most of the 20 minutes: a lid traps steam and slows reduction, and a hard boil does not thicken faster at this volume but can break the mince into a grainy texture. Remember the filling thickens a little more as it stands, so judge it slightly looser than your final target — but only slightly.

Checking the seasoning before assembly

Taste the filling at the end of Step 5, once it has cooled for a few seconds. Ask three questions: is it salty enough, does it taste flat, and does anything dominate? Flat usually means salt or acidity; a little more Worcestershire sauce fixes the acidity. Dominance usually means too much of one herb, which is hard to reverse, so add herbs in the stated quantities first. Do this now — after assembly, the only seasoning you can still adjust is on the mash.

Why a watery filling causes problems

A watery filling does not stay under the mash. It soaks into the base of the potato, turning it grey and slack, and it bubbles up through the topping and spills over the dish. You get soup at the bottom and dry potato on top, instead of two distinct layers. Reducing the filling properly prevents all of it, and makes the rest of the dish much easier.

How to make the mashed potato topping well

Cutting and cooking the potatoes

Cut the potatoes into similar chunks, about 4 cm. Even chunks finish together; if some are much smaller, they break down into the water while the large ones are still hard in the middle, and that waterlogged potato is one cause of gluey mash. Start them in cold, well-salted water so they heat through evenly and absorb seasoning as they cook, and keep the water at a simmer rather than a rolling boil, which bashes the chunks apart. Test the largest chunk, not the smallest: a knife should meet no resistance and no chalky core. If in doubt, cook for two more minutes — slightly overcooked floury potatoes still mash well; undercooked ones never do.

Draining and drying

Drain the potatoes as soon as they are ready; do not leave them sitting in their cooking water, as they keep absorbing it and turn heavy. The minute back over a low heat is the most valuable minute in the topping. You should see steam rising and the surfaces looking matte and floury rather than shiny and wet. Skip it, and the mash needs less milk, browns less, and is more likely to slump.

Adding butter and milk, and avoiding gluey mash

Mash the butter in first — it coats the potato and gives a smoother result than adding butter and milk together. Then add warm milk a splash at a time, beating after each addition, and stop as soon as the mash is smooth and spreadable. You may not need all 75ml; varieties and cooking times vary. Gluey mash is usually overworked or made from the wrong potato: a food processor or electric whisk breaks the cells down too far and releases starch, turning the mash elastic. Use a hand masher, or a ricer if you have one, and work only until the lumps are gone. Once mash has turned gluey it cannot be reversed, so the remedy is prevention and a lighter hand.

How thick the mash should be

The finished mash should be soft but self-supporting. Lift a spoonful and turn the spoon sideways: the mash should hold its shape for a moment before settling. If it pours or slumps flat at once, it is too wet to top a pie well. If it stands in stiff peaks and will not spread, it is too dry — add a splash more milk. Spread it while warm; cold mash is stiff, tears the surface of the filling, and is far harder to seal to the edges.

Assembling and baking in more detail

Preparing the dish and adding the filling

You do not need to grease the dish; the filling contains enough fat to stop it sticking badly. Check it is ovenproof and the size you think it is — if unsure, measure a litre of water into it. Put the empty dish on a baking tray before you fill it: a full, hot dish is awkward to balance, and the tray catches any overflow. Spoon the filling in, level it, and push it into the corners so there are no air gaps. It should sit about 2.5 cm deep, with the mash bringing the finished pie to about 4.5 to 5 cm, and be warm rather than boiling.

Should the filling cool completely before adding the mash? No. It should stop steaming fiercely, but it does not need to be cold. Warm filling under warm mash bakes evenly and keeps the layers distinct. Cold filling is a different case and needs longer in the oven — see Making Ahead.

Spreading the mash and forking the top

Dollop the mash on in spoonfuls, starting at the edges. This is not fussiness: starting in the middle and dragging outwards pulls the filling up through the potato. Spread with the back of a spoon using short, light strokes, and work the mash right to the sides — that seal matters, because an open gap is where the gravy escapes and bubbles through. If a little filling shows through, patch it with a small spoonful of mash. Then draw a fork across the surface in lines, swirls or a crosshatch, pressing lightly: you want texture, not furrows down to the filling. The thin edges of those ridges dry and colour first, and give the top its crispness. If using cheese, scatter it evenly over the forked surface and check the pie a few minutes earlier, as cheese browns faster than potato alone.

Position, bubbling and checking the centre

Use the middle shelf for the most even heat, and leave space around the dish where you can — a dish pushed against the back wall of a small oven often browns unevenly on that side. The filling will bubble as it heats; around the edges, that is your sign of readiness. Leave at least 1 cm between the top of the mash and the rim to avoid a boil-over. Colour alone is not a reliable test: look for steady bubbling right around the edges. With a food probe, the centre should be steaming hot; without one, push a thin knife into the centre, leave it a few seconds, and touch it carefully to your lip or wrist — it should feel properly hot, not warm. If the top is done but the centre is not, cover loosely with foil and bake 10 minutes more.

Resting before serving

Rest every version of this pie for at least 5 minutes. The filling is at its loosest straight from the oven, and resting lets the gravy settle back around the mince so portions hold together. A dish of this size holds its heat well, so resting will not make it cold.

Practical tips and common mistakes

Thin gravy

Cause: too much stock, too short a simmer, or a lid left on the pan. Remedy: simmer uncovered until a spoon leaves a slow-closing trail. For a filling that is thin before assembly, mix 1 tablespoon of cornflour with 2 tablespoons of cold water, stir it in, and simmer for 2 minutes. Once the pie is assembled this cannot be done, so prevention matters most. The FAQs page summarises this fix.

Bland filling

Cause: under-seasoning, under-browned mince, or assuming salty stock is enough on its own. Remedy: brown the mince properly, then taste at the end of cooking and adjust — salt first, then a little more Worcestershire sauce if it still tastes flat.

Lumpy mash and gluey mash

Lumps come from unevenly cut or not-quite-cooked potatoes; test the largest chunk before draining, because hard lumps from undercooking cannot be mashed out. Gluey mash comes from a waxy variety or from a food processor or electric whisk; use floury potatoes and a hand masher, and work them only until smooth.

Mash sinking into the filling

Cause: the filling was too thin, or too hot, when the mash went on; wet mash makes it worse. Remedy: reduce the filling, let it stop steaming fiercely, make the mash firm, and dollop the potato on from the edges instead of dropping it into the centre of a liquid filling.

A pale topping and filling bubbling over

A pale top usually means wet mash, a smooth surface, an oven that was not fully heated, or a dish placed too low. Dry the potatoes well, fork the surface, use the middle shelf, and finish with 2 to 3 minutes under a hot grill if needed. Bubbling over usually means an overfilled dish or a thinner filling than it looked; leave 1 cm of headroom and always bake on a tray. It is not ruined if it does bubble — let the pie rest and the overflow settles back at the edges.

The wrong dish size

Measure the capacity with water if you are unsure. In a deep, narrow dish, add time and check the centre carefully, because heat takes longer to reach it. In a wide, shallow dish, check early, because a thin filling dries out faster.

Substitutions and variations

The options below keep the structure of the basic recipe. Where a change alters the identity of the dish, that is stated plainly. Testing status: these are suggestions based on standard cooking practice and have not been separately tested alongside this recipe. Treat the first attempt as a test, and expect small adjustments to liquid and seasoning. Full detail is on the Variations page.

SwapHow to use itWhat changes
Gluten-freeReplace the plain flour with cornflour mixed with cold water, stirred into the simmering filling near the end. Check the labels of your stock and Worcestershire sauce — some brands are gluten-free and some are not, and formulations change.A glossier, slightly clearer sauce than flour gives. Cooking time stays the same.
Dairy-free mashSwap the butter for a dairy-free spread or a tablespoon of olive oil, and the milk for an unsweetened plant milk or a few spoonfuls of potato cooking water.Unsweetened is essential. Add liquid even more gradually — some alternatives slacken the mash suddenly.
Extra vegetablesFinely diced mushrooms, leeks, swede or parsnip. Hard vegetables go in with the carrot and celery; leeks with the onion; mushrooms after the mince has browned, with a few minutes to release their water.Mushrooms and courgette release water, so you may need a longer simmer. Root vegetables absorb a little, so the filling may need a splash more stock.
Cheese toppingScatter 50g grated mature Cheddar over the forked mash; season the mash itself a fraction more lightly, as the cheese adds salt.A richer, more deeply browned top. Not required, and not traditional in a stricter sense.
Lamb minceSame quantity and method; lamb or chicken stock suits it better than beef stock.The dish becomes shepherd's pie. It is no longer a cottage pie.
Turkey minceSame quantity; brown it well, as it colours less readily. Keep the full simmer and do not reduce the stock further.A leaner filling that can dry out.
LentilsFor half-and-half, use 250g mince and about 200g cooked green or Puy lentils, added near the end of simmering. For meat-free, use about 400g cooked lentils, vegetable stock, and leave out the Worcestershire sauce or use a vegetarian alternative, because the standard sauce contains fish.Call it a lentil cottage pie. Choose lentils that hold their shape — red lentils break down completely and are not suitable here.
Red wine (optional)Pour in about 125ml after the tomato purée stage, bubble for 2 to 3 minutes, and reduce the stock by the same amount.A deeper, slightly sharper flavour. The recipe does not need it.

What to serve with cottage pie

Cottage pie is a complete dish: it already contains meat, sauce and potato, so the sides that work best are simple and green. Buttered cabbage is the classic partner — mild, good at soaking up gravy, and a contrast to the richness. Green beans and peas do the same job with a fresher taste, and broccoli works well cooked until just tender. In warmer weather, a plain green salad gives a crisp contrast to a soft, rich pie. Avoid serving more potato in another form; chips or roast potatoes next to a mashed potato topping make the plate heavy and repetitive. Extra gravy is a matter of taste — this filling is well sauced, so make a small jug separately rather than thinning the filling to provide it.

Making ahead, storing, freezing and reheating

The safety points below follow current UK food safety guidance (Food Standards Agency and Food Standards Scotland, checked 27 October 2026) and are set out separately from the texture advice, because the two are not the same thing.

Preparing components and assembling ahead

Can cottage pie be assembled in advance? Yes. You can make the filling a day ahead — cool it, cover it and refrigerate it; the flavour often improves overnight. Mash can also be made ahead, although it is best fresh. Press cling film directly onto the surface and refrigerate it. Before spreading, let it come back towards room temperature, or warm it gently with a splash of milk. Assembling from cold components is easier in one way, as cold mash spreads over cold filling without the layers mixing. Bake a chilled, assembled pie at 200°C conventional / 180°C fan / Gas Mark 6 for about 35 to 40 minutes (estimate), checking the centre with the knife test above.

Cooling and refrigeration

Cool cooked food as quickly as you reasonably can — ideally within one to two hours — then store it in the fridge, which should be between 0°C and 5°C. Splitting a large pie into smaller portions helps it cool faster, as a deep whole pie holds heat in the centre for a long time. Eat refrigerated leftovers within two days. Cover the dish or transfer portions to sealed containers, and label them with the date.

Freezing and defrosting

Cottage pie freezes well assembled but unbaked, or cooked and completely cooled. Portions freeze and defrost more evenly than a whole large pie; wrap well or use sealed freezer containers and label with the date. An unbaked frozen pie gives the best topping texture, because the potato is baked once, from defrosted. Defrost thoroughly in the fridge — overnight for a whole pie, several hours for a portion — and cook and eat within 24 hours of defrosting. Do not refreeze a defrosted pie, and do not defrost it on the worktop all day.

Reheating

Reheat leftovers only once, until steaming hot all the way through with no cold centre. For a portion in the oven, use 180°C conventional / 160°C fan / Gas Mark 4 for about 25 to 30 minutes, covered with foil for the first half so the top does not dry out, then uncovered to crisp again. In the microwave, use short bursts and stir or turn the portion partway through if the dish allows — mashed potato heats unevenly, so a single long blast can leave a cold patch in the middle of a very hot portion. Always check the centre: steaming at the edges is not enough on its own. This recipe is written to be defrosted first; no from-frozen cooking time is given, because defrosting in the fridge gives an even result and lets you check the centre reliably.

Scaling the recipe up or down

Halving

Use 250g of mince and half of everything else. Brown in a smaller pan if you have one, so the mince still has room. Use a smaller dish of roughly 750ml to 1 litre, so the layers stay at a similar depth — a half quantity spread across the full-size dish makes a thin pie that dries out. Baking time stays similar, perhaps 5 minutes less; judge by bubbling at the edges and a properly hot centre, not by halving the clock. Taste and adjust the seasoning rather than assuming halved salt is exactly right.

Doubling

Use 1kg of mince and double the other quantities. Brown the mince in two or three batches, without exception — a kilo in one pan will steam, and the whole dish will suffer for it. Use a much larger dish of 3 to 4 litres, or split the pie between two dishes of the usual size, which is often easier: they heat more evenly, are lighter to lift, and one can be frozen. Do not double the baking time; a deeper filling needs perhaps 10 to 15 minutes more for its centre, and the top would burn if you simply doubled the time — cover with foil if the top colours first. Double the herbs, but add salt in stages. Two dishes need space between them for hot air to move; if they touch, or one is directly above the other, swap them around halfway through.

Frequently asked questions

These questions were chosen because they fit this recipe. They were not taken from any search feature, and are not presented as Google People Also Ask questions.

No. Cheese is an optional topping, not a defining ingredient. Plain mashed potato, properly forked and baked, gives the traditional top. Add 50g grated mature Cheddar if you want a richer, more deeply browned finish.

Warm it gently with a splash of milk first so it spreads without tearing the filling, and check its consistency — very soft leftover mash can slump. It must be piping hot by the end of baking, like the rest of the pie.

Floury varieties — Maris Piper and King Edward are the reliable choices, and most large supermarkets stock both. They break down as they cook, so they mash smoothly. Waxy and salad potatoes hold their shape instead, which makes them a poor fit for a topping.

Dry the potatoes: drain them well, return them to the hot pan for a minute to steam off, and add the milk gradually. Also reduce the filling properly before the mash goes on — a watery top is usually a watery filling showing through, wet potatoes, or both.

Yes. Divide the filling between ramekins or small ovenproof dishes, top each with mash, and fork the surfaces in the same way. They bake faster than one large pie — roughly 15 to 20 minutes with hot components (estimate) — so check the centre of one portion before serving the rest.

Yes, if it has been defrosted safely in the fridge first. Cook it as soon as it has thawed and brown it thoroughly, with no pink remaining. Frozen mince releases more liquid in the pan than fresh — pour off the excess and keep browning, or the filling will start thin and need a longer simmer.

Usually because the dish was overfilled, or the filling was thinner than it looked. Leave at least 1 cm between the top of the mash and the rim, and always stand the dish on a baking tray. A small amount of bubbling at the edges is normal and is your sign the pie is ready.

This recipe is written to be defrosted first, then baked or reheated. Defrosting in the fridge gives an even result and lets you check the centre reliably, so no from-frozen time is given here. Thaw thoroughly, then use the chilled-pie time in the making-ahead section.

No, although they are close relations. Cumberland pie also has a mashed potato topping, but it is traditionally finished with breadcrumbs and cheese over the potato. Add the optional cheese and a handful of breadcrumbs here and you are moving towards a Cumberland pie; without the breadcrumbs, it stays a cottage pie.

Cottage Pie Variations

Eight adaptations of the main cottage pie recipe. Each one starts from that recipe — the quantities and method there are the base, and only the changes are described here.

Testing status: these are adaptation suggestions based on standard cooking practice. They have not been fully developed and tested as separate recipes, so treat a first attempt as a test and expect small adjustments to liquid and seasoning.

Cheese-topped cottage pie

What changes: 50g grated mature Cheddar scattered over the forked mash before baking. Nothing else changes. Why it matters: the cheese adds salt and richness and browns faster than potato alone, so check the pie a few minutes earlier than the recipe time if your oven runs hot, and season the mash itself a fraction more lightly.

Texture and flavour: a crisper, more deeply coloured top with a savoury, slightly sharp flavour. Identity: still a cottage pie, but not traditional in a stricter sense — many traditional versions have no cheese at all. Testing needed: yes, as an untested suggestion; the main variables are browning time and salt balance.

Extra-vegetable cottage pie

What changes: add finely diced mushrooms, leeks, swede or parsnip to the filling. Why it matters: every additional vegetable changes the liquid in the dish, which is the thing cottage pie is most sensitive to.

Ingredient and method adjustments: add hard vegetables such as swede and parsnip with the carrot and celery; add leeks with the onion; add mushrooms after the mince has browned and give them a few minutes to release their water before the stock goes in. Mushrooms and courgette release water, so allow a longer simmer rather than extra stock. Root vegetables absorb a little liquid, so the filling may need a splash more stock.

Texture and flavour: a looser-textured, more varied filling with more sweetness from root vegetables. Identity: still a cottage pie. Testing needed: yes — final liquid after simmering is the point to check.

Individual portions

What changes: the filling is divided between ramekins or small ovenproof dishes and each is topped and forked separately. Why it matters: small pies heat through faster, freeze and defrost in portions, and suit households eating at different times. Everyone also gets crisp edges.

Method adjustments: allow roughly 15 to 20 minutes of baking for small pies assembled with hot components (estimate), and check the centre of one portion before serving the rest. Keep the same filling thickness check before topping — a thin filling behaves the same at any size. Testing needed: yes, particularly the baking time for your ramekin size.

Gluten-free adaptation

What changes: the plain flour is replaced with cornflour, and two other ingredients must be checked rather than assumed safe. Why it matters: gluten in this dish is not only in the flour.

Ingredient adjustments: do not add cornflour at the flour stage. Instead, mix 1 tablespoon of cornflour with 2 tablespoons of cold water and stir it into the simmering filling near the end, then simmer for 2 minutes. Then check the label of your stock and the label of your Worcestershire sauce: some brands are gluten-free and some are not, and formulations change. Do not assume any stock, gravy product or sauce is gluten-free without reading its label.

Texture and flavour: cornflour gives a glossier, slightly clearer sauce than flour; the flavour is otherwise unchanged and the cooking time stays the same. Testing needed: yes — check the sauce thickness at the quantity above.

Dairy-free topping

What changes: the butter and milk in the mash only; the filling is unchanged. Why it matters: the topping's liquid behaviour changes, and a sweetened alternative will flavour a savoury pie in a way that does not suit it.

Ingredient adjustments: swap the butter for a dairy-free spread or a tablespoon of olive oil, and the milk for an unsweetened plant milk, or for a few spoonfuls of the potato cooking water. Add the liquid even more gradually than usual, because some alternatives make the mash slacken suddenly.

Texture and flavour: slightly less rich, and softer if the liquid goes in too fast. Drying the potatoes thoroughly (Step 7 of the recipe) matters even more here. Testing needed: yes, for liquid quantity.

Lentil / vegetarian adaptation

What changes: cooked green or Puy lentils replace some or all of the mince. For a half-and-half filling, use 250g beef mince and about 200g cooked lentils, added near the end of simmering. For a fully meat-free version, leave the mince out, use around 400g cooked lentils and vegetable stock, and leave out the Worcestershire sauce or use a vegetarian alternative — the standard sauce traditionally contains fish (anchovy), so a version using it is not vegetarian.

Why it matters: lentil choice decides the texture. Green and Puy lentils hold their shape. Red lentils break down completely and turn the filling into a purée, so they are not suitable here. Lentils also absorb liquid, so add a splash more stock if the filling looks dry.

Texture and flavour: a softer, earthier filling without the browned-meat depth, which makes thorough seasoning and the tomato purée stage more important. Identity: this changes the traditional identity of the dish. Call it a lentil cottage pie, so readers know what they are making. Testing needed: yes, as a separate formulation.

Slow cooker cottage pie

What changes: the filling is cooked in a slow cooker instead of simmered on the hob; the pie is still topped with mash and finished in the oven. Why it matters: a slow cooker traps moisture, so the filling reduces far less than it does in an open pan — the liquid quantity is the whole adaptation.

Ingredient and method adjustments: brown the mince and soften the vegetables on the hob first, exactly as in Steps 1 to 3 of the main recipe — a slow cooker does not brown, and skipping this stage gives a pale, steamed-tasting filling. Transfer to the slow cooker with the stock reduced to about 250ml, then cook on low until the beef is tender. Check the consistency before assembly: if it is thinner than the spoon-trail test in the recipe, simmer it briefly in a pan or stir in the cornflour mixture from the gluten-free adaptation. Make the mash as usual, assemble, and bake as usual so the top browns — a slow cooker cannot do that part.

Texture and flavour: a softer, more melded filling; the vegetables partly melt into the gravy. Identity: still a cottage pie once it is topped and baked. Testing needed: yes — cooker models vary widely, so no single slow-cooker time is stated here; treat the first attempt as a test and judge by tenderness and thickness, not the clock.

Cauliflower mash topping

What changes: part or all of the potato in the topping is replaced with cauliflower. Why it matters: cauliflower holds much more water than potato and has far less starch, so the topping behaves differently — wetter, softer, and less able to hold forked ridges.

Ingredient and method adjustments: for a half-and-half topping, use about 450g potato and 450g cauliflower florets. Cook the cauliflower until completely tender, then drain it very thoroughly and let it steam dry for several minutes — longer than you would dry potatoes. Mash it with the potato, butter and only a splash of milk at first; many batches need no extra milk at all. A full cauliflower topping is possible but slumps and browns unevenly, so half-and-half is the safer starting point.

Texture and flavour: lighter and softer, with a mild cauliflower flavour that is noticeable but not dominant in the half-and-half version. Dietary note: this swap is sometimes made by readers reducing carbohydrate, but no nutrition figures are stated for it here, because none have been calculated for this formulation. Testing needed: yes, particularly the liquid quantity.

Questions about the variations

The cheese-topped version. One ingredient is scattered over the mash before baking, and nothing else in the recipe changes. It is the place to start if you want to change one thing at a time.

Often, yes — cheese on top of an extra-vegetable filling, for example, or a dairy-free topping on individual portions. Bear in mind that each change can affect the liquid in the filling and the salt in the dish, and that these adaptations are untested suggestions. Treat a first combined attempt as a test, and change one thing back if the result is not right.

No. Every variation on this page uses the main recipe's oven temperature unless its own section says otherwise. What can change is the time: small individual portions bake faster, and a cheese topping browns sooner, so check those pies a few minutes early.

Work through every ingredient, not just the obvious one. Each dietary adaptation on this page flags the ingredients that need checking — in this recipe, usually the stock and the Worcestershire sauce — because brands differ and formulations change. Always read the label of the product you actually have.

Cooking and assembly

Variations

The meat: beef for cottage pie, lamb for shepherd's pie. The method is much the same.

Make-ahead preparation and leftovers

Cool leftovers ideally within one to two hours, refrigerate (fridge 0–5°C), and eat within two days. Reheat only once, until steaming hot all the way through with no cold centre. Yes — assembled and unbaked, or cooked and completely cooled. Portions defrost more evenly than a whole pie. Defrost thoroughly in the fridge and cook and eat within 24 hours of defrosting. Do not refreeze a defrosted pie.

Website timer and printing

About Us

cottagepierecipe.uk is a website about one dish: cottage pie, covered thoroughly and honestly.

What this site is for

The site exists to help home cooks in the United Kingdom make a good cottage pie, and to fix it when it goes wrong. It does that with one complete recipe, a page of genuine variations, troubleshooting inside the recipe itself, and a set of short answers. There is also a working cooking timer on every page, because timing is part of cooking the dish.

Who it helps

Anyone cooking cottage pie at home: people making it for the first time who want the steps in the right order, and people who have made it before and want to know why the filling was watery, the mash sank, or the top stayed pale.

How the recipes are written

Quantities are given in grams and millilitres. Oven temperatures are given in Celsius for conventional and fan ovens, with the Gas Mark alongside. Instructions include the visual and texture cues that tell you how a stage is going — what the gravy should look like, how the mash should behave on a spoon — because a clock alone cannot tell you that. Substitutions are labelled as tested or as suggestions, and those are never mixed up. Food-safety guidance follows current UK sources, which are named on the page where the guidance appears.

Who writes it

This site is written and run by Michael. No biography or qualifications are claimed beyond what is stated on this page.

The main cottage pie recipe was kitchen-tested by Michael, the site owner, in October 2026: cooked exactly as written, and it turned out as described. [Further recipe development and testing details — to be supplied.]

Feedback and corrections

Corrections are welcome and are acted on. If a quantity, time or instruction looks wrong, or a result did not match the page, use the Contact page and choose “Recipe correction”. Please include the page address and what happened. Confirmed corrections are made to the page, and safety-related corrections take priority over everything else.

Questions about this website and how it is run

The site is written and run by Michael. It is a one-person project about one dish — no chef, team or professional history is claimed.

Depth over breadth. One dish means the recipe, its variations, its common failures and its storage guidance can all be covered properly, instead of hundreds of recipes each covered thinly.

Yes. The site owner cooked it exactly as written in October 2026, and it turned out as described — the recipe page says so at the top. Anything that has not been tested, such as the variations, is labelled a suggestion rather than a finished recipe.

No. No ratings or reviews have been collected, so none are shown — on the recipe, in the cards on the homepage, or in the pages' structured data.

Home › Disclaimer

Disclaimer

Recipe outcomes

Recipes are written as clearly as we can make them, but results depend on your ingredients, equipment, oven and judgement. Ovens vary; use the visual and texture cues on each page alongside the times given. A disclaimer does not excuse an inaccurate or unsafe instruction — if you find one, please report it through the Contact page so it can be corrected.

Testing status

Where a recipe or variation has not been tested, the page says so plainly and labels its times as estimates. Untested content must not be described elsewhere as tried-and-tested.

Substitutions and dietary information

Substitutions change flavour, texture and sometimes the identity of a dish; pages explain which. Dietary labels are used cautiously: ingredient formulations vary by brand and change over time, so always check the label of the product you actually have, especially for allergens and gluten. Nothing on this site is medical or dietary advice.

Nutrition

No nutrition figures are published for recipes on this site unless they have been calculated for that exact formulation. Figures published for other recipes elsewhere do not apply to the recipes here and must not be assumed to.

Food safety

Storage, chilling, freezing and reheating guidance is drawn from current UK food safety sources, which are named on the relevant pages. Guidance changes; the source, not this summary, is the authority.

Third-party links

Links to other websites are provided for reference. We do not control their content and are not responsible for it. A link is not an endorsement of a product.

Affiliates and sponsorship

There are no affiliate links or sponsored relationships on this website at present. If that changes, the affected pages will disclose it.

Questions about this disclaimer

Five things: that recipe results vary with your ingredients, equipment and oven; that untested content is labelled as such; that substitutions and dietary notes need care; that no nutrition figures are published without calculation; and that links to other websites are not endorsements.

No. The disclaimer covers genuine variation in home cooking. It does not excuse an inaccurate or unsafe instruction — if you find one, please report it through the Contact page so it can be corrected.

Because none have been calculated for these exact formulations. Figures published for other recipes elsewhere do not apply here, and guessing at numbers would be worse than publishing none.

No. Ingredient formulations vary by brand and change over time. The pages flag what to check, but the label of the product you actually have is what decides — especially for allergens and gluten.
